paper.title: Working Hours, Top Management Appointments, and Gender: Evidence from Linked Employer-Employee Data
paper.code_data_availability: Data Availability (p. 921): "Code replicating the tables and figures in this article can be found in Frederiksen, Kato, and Smith (2024) in the Harvard Dataverse, https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/UT2AL6." No Statistics Denmark project number is …

registers.name_in_paper: the Integrated Database for Labor Market Research (IDA)
registers.role: sample frame, outcome (job level: top manager vs. manager, hence the appointment indicator), firm characteristics, linkage
treatment: actual and usual weekly working hours, nonstandard (evening/night/weekend) hours, and the repeated hours observation h2 from the follow-up interview
variables_mentioned: actual weekly hours (hours actually worked in the last week)
usual weekly hours (hours usually worked per week)

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish Time Use Surveys (2001 and 2008), collected by the Danish Center for Social Science Research
registers.role: supply-side evidence on household production: 10-minute weekday and weekend diaries for supervisory managers and their spouses (figs. 3 and 4)

linkages: DLFS respondents merged with IDA register records by person ID, so that surveyed individuals can be followed beyond the time of the survey
firm IDs in the register merged onto DLFS person IDs to identify all DLFS respondents employed by the same company in a given year, which defines the peer group used for 'longest hours among peers'
the DLFS panel component links the initial hours observation h1 to the follow-up observation h2 collected 13 weeks later for the same individual
spouses linked within households in the Danish Time Use Surveys, each spouse filling out diaries for the same days

sample.universe: Workers in Denmark sampled by the Danish Labor Force Survey between 1996 and 2018 (189,121 employees) and merged with the IDA register; the analysis sample is the managers among them
selection_rules: Use organizational hierarchy codes in the register data to identify, for each year, all workers who are either 'top managers' or 'managers'
Managers include all workers who hold management positions, excluding top managers
The DLFS sample contains 47,859 individuals: 8,009 top managers and 39,850 managers
The estimation sample is the 39,850 managers; incumbent top managers are excluded because they cannot be appointed
Of those 39,850 managers, 410 receive a top management appointment between t and t + 1 (237 internal promotions, 173 external recruitments)
Main specification uses the initial DLFS hours observation (h1), collected in a random week of the year and linked to register data collected each November
Robustness sample A: exclude individuals with multiple employers in a given year, N = 27,726
Robustness sample B: exclude observations whose interview week is more than 6 months from November, N = 28,809
Table 7 sample: managers for whom a company peer group can be constructed from other DLFS respondents, N = 25,016
Table 9 sample: managers with both h1 and the follow-up hours observation h2 collected 13 weeks later, N = 24,679

Time use analysis: 934 married supervisory managers whose spouses are not supervisory managers, plus 133 power couples in which both spouses are supervisory managers, from the 10,624 households of the 2001 and 2008 Danish Time Use Surveys
sample.n_observations: 39,850 manager-year observations in the baseline estimation sample
sample.n_individuals: 47,859 individuals in the DLFS sample (8,009 top managers and 39,850 managers), drawn from the 189,121 Danish employees the DLFS sampled between 1996 and 2018

construction_notes: Hours enter the linear specification as h/100; the reported coefficients throughout are logit marginal effects, not log-odds coefficients
The nonlinear specification replaces hours with dummies 0 < h < 37, 38 <= h <= 47 and h >= 48; the omitted reference category is working the standard Danish workweek of exactly 37 hours

Every specification is reported twice, once with actual weekly hours (hours actually worked in the last week) and once with usual weekly hours (hours usually worked per week); usual hours are noted as more subject to recall bias, actual hours as a single-week measure
The DLFS defines 'regularly' as more than half of the working days in the 4-week period and 'sometimes' as at least once within the 4-week period but less than half of the working days

The register hours measure (Lonstatistikken) was rejected because it records the hours employers are contractually obliged to pay for, which misses the unpaid overtime of managers on funktionaeroverenskomst contracts

DLFS interviews fall in a random week of the year while the register data are collected each November; one robustness specification weights observations so that importance decreases linearly with the distance to November

h2 is the hours observation from the follow-up DLFS interview 13 weeks after the initial one; 24.26% of h2 observations cross over to the following year; the correlation between h1 and h2 is 0.45 for actual hours and 0.67 for usual hours
Figure 2 follows Gicheva (2013, fig. 4): the appointment dummy is regressed on all covariates except hours and the residual is plotted against hours, with 90% confidence intervals

The control list differs slightly between the text of eq. (1) on p. 903 (quadratics in age, tenure and experience; age of oldest child) and the note to table 4 (quadratics in age, tenure, experience and number of children); table 10 shows the cumulative order in which the blocks enter
The average annual probability of a top management appointment for managers is 1.0%; for male managers it is 1.20% and for female managers 0.48%

claims.statement: Among Danish managers, a 100-hour increase in actual weekly working hours (h/100) raises the annual probability of a top management appointment, estimated as a logit marginal effect in Table 4, column (1).

treatment.label: h/100 (actual weekly working hours divided by 100)

register_source.value: DLFS (Danish Labour Force Survey), weekly working hours; the DLFS record is merged to the IDA register by person ID

definition.value: Actual weekly working hours, i.e., the number of hours actually worked in the last week, as reported by manager i at the initial DLFS interview in year t. Entered linearly as hours/100 in the baseline logit, equation (1).

timing.value: year t, before the appointment measured between t and t + 1

outcome.label: appoint (top management appointment between year t and year t + 1)

register_source.value: IDA (Integrated Database for Labor Market Research): organizational hierarchy codes identifying each worker's job level (top manager / manager) in each year

definition.value: appoint_it = 1 if manager i is appointed to a top management position between year t and year t + 1 (i.e., manager i's job level is manager in year t and top manager in year t + 1) and 0 otherwise. Top managers are defined from organizational hierarchy codes and are described by the authors as comparable to the top management team or C-class executives in large US firms.

timing.value: measured over the year following the year t in which hours are reported

units.value: change in the annual probability of a top management appointment per unit of h/100, i.e., per 100 actual weekly working hours (logit marginal effect)

magnitude.interpretation: An increase in actual working hours of 1 standard deviation (11 hours) raises the annual odds of a top management appointment by 0.25 percentage points, a 25% increase from 1.0% to 1.25%.

estimand.target_population: Danish managers (workers in management positions who are not yet top managers) observed in the DLFS and merged with IDA; the quantity is a covariate-adjusted logit marginal effect, which the paper describes as an association rather than an experimentally identified effect
estimand.time_horizon: appointment occurring between year t and year t + 1, with hours measured in year t

population.description: Managers (all workers holding management positions, excluding top managers) in the DLFS merged with IDA; incumbent top managers excluded. N = 39,850.
population.selection: The DLFS randomly samples Danish employees; the estimation sample conditions on holding a management position (but not a top management position) in year t.

identification.source_of_variation: cross-sectional and over-time variation in self-reported weekly working hours among managers who are observationally comparable on a comprehensive set of individual and firm covariates; there is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates of equation (1) — quadratics in age, tenure, experience and number of children, education, gender, cohabiting/marriage, public sector and exporting status, company sales and size, industry, two-digit occupation and year fixed effects — working hours are independent of the unobserved determinants of a top management appointment, so that the estimated marginal effect is not driven by omitted worker or firm characteristics.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reports its result as holding 'after controlling for a comprehensive set of covariates' and shows in table 10 how a coefficient moves as covariate blocks are added sequentially, but it never states an unconfoundedness condition and describes its finding as an association.

key_assumptions.assumption: Hours are measured before the appointment, so the appointment cannot have produced the reported hours and managers do not adjust hours in anticipation of an appointment already decided.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper notes that managers report their hours in year t before becoming top managers in year t + 1; footnote 12 further reports that mean hours do not rise after appointment (42.02 before vs. 40.84 after, actual hours).

key_assumptions.assumption: Weekly hours reported for a single DLFS interview week (actual hours), or recalled as usual hours, measure the working hours that are relevant to the firm's top management appointment decision.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Every result is reported for both actual and usual hours; table 5 shows robustness to dropping multiple-employer observations, to weighting observations by distance from November, and to dropping interview weeks more than 6 months from November.

threats_discussed: the hours observed in the DLFS interview week may come from, or be contaminated by, an employment relationship other than the one observed in the November register data
working hour observations more distant from November may be less relevant to the appointment decision
usual hours are more subject to measurement error (such as recall bias) than actual hours
robustness_checks: table 5, cols. 3-4: reestimation excluding individuals with multiple employers in a given year (N = 27,726)
table 5, cols. 5-6: observations weighted so that importance decreases linearly with the distance of the interview week to November
table 5, cols. 7-8: excluding observations more than 6 months from November (N = 28,809)
every specification reported for both actual and usual hours
every specification reported in a linear (h/100) and a nonlinear (hours-category dummy) form
table 9, cols. 1-4: table 4 reestimated on the restricted sample that has both h1 and h2, to show the restriction is inconsequential
a version of table 9 excluding individuals whose h2 crosses over to the following year (reported as qualitatively similar, not shown)

estimation.specification: equation (1), the baseline logit of a top management appointment on hours and controls

source_table.value: Table 4, col. (1), row 'h/100 (actual weekly hours / 100)'

heterogeneity.dimension: private vs. public sector
heterogeneity.finding: the effect of hours on promotion is present in both sectors but stronger in the private sector (fn. 14, not tabulated)

heterogeneity.dimension: industry and sector
heterogeneity.finding: fig. 1 shows the marginal effect of hours varies widely across industries, and predominantly female industries (public sector, education, health care) reward long working hours less

heterogeneity.dimension: gender
heterogeneity.finding: the hours-career profiles of men and women do not differ significantly in slope (fig. 2), and gender-dummy x hours interactions are insignificant

claims.statement: Among Danish managers, being the longest-working individual in the firm peer group (ranked on usual hours) raises the annual probability of a top management appointment, estimated as a logit marginal effect in Table 7, panel A, column (4).

treatment.label: longest hours among peers

register_source.value: IDA firm identifier merged to the DLFS by person ID, used to identify every DLFS respondent employed by the same company in the same year; hours from the DLFS

definition.value: longest hours among peers_it = 1 if worker i in year t is the individual with the longest working hours in his/her peer group in year t, and 0 otherwise. The peer group is all other DLFS respondents employed by the same company in the same year, identified by matching DLFS person IDs to register firm IDs. Measured with usual hours.

timing.value: year t, before the appointment measured between t and t + 1

outcome.label: appoint (top management appointment between year t and year t + 1)

register_source.value: IDA (Integrated Database for Labor Market Research): organizational hierarchy codes identifying each worker's job level (top manager / manager) in each year

definition.value: appoint_it = 1 if manager i is appointed to a top management position between year t and year t + 1 (i.e., manager i's job level is manager in year t and top manager in year t + 1) and 0 otherwise. Top managers are defined from organizational hierarchy codes and are described by the authors as comparable to the top management team or C-class executives in large US firms.

timing.value: measured over the year following the year t in which hours are reported

units.value: change in the annual probability of a top management appointment from being the longest-working individual in the firm peer group rather than not (logit marginal effect)

estimand.target_population: Danish managers (workers in management positions who are not yet top managers) observed in the DLFS and merged with IDA; the quantity is a covariate-adjusted logit marginal effect, which the paper describes as an association rather than an experimentally identified effect
estimand.time_horizon: appointment occurring between year t and year t + 1, with hours measured in year t

population.description: Managers for whom a peer group (other DLFS respondents employed by the same company in the same year) can be constructed, so that 'longest hours among peers' is non-missing. N = 25,016.
population.selection: Conditions on at least one other DLFS respondent being employed by the same company in the same year, so that a peer-group hours ranking exists.

identification.source_of_variation: cross-sectional and over-time variation in self-reported weekly working hours among managers who are observationally comparable on a comprehensive set of individual and firm covariates; there is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates of equation (1) — quadratics in age, tenure, experience and number of children, education, gender, cohabiting/marriage, public sector and exporting status, company sales and size, industry, two-digit occupation and year fixed effects — working hours are independent of the unobserved determinants of a top management appointment, so that the estimated marginal effect is not driven by omitted worker or firm characteristics.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reports its result as holding 'after controlling for a comprehensive set of covariates' and shows in table 10 how a coefficient moves as covariate blocks are added sequentially, but it never states an unconfoundedness condition and describes its finding as an association.

key_assumptions.assumption: Hours are measured before the appointment, so the appointment cannot have produced the reported hours and managers do not adjust hours in anticipation of an appointment already decided.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper notes that managers report their hours in year t before becoming top managers in year t + 1; footnote 12 further reports that mean hours do not rise after appointment (42.02 before vs. 40.84 after, actual hours).

key_assumptions.assumption: Weekly hours reported for a single DLFS interview week (actual hours), or recalled as usual hours, measure the working hours that are relevant to the firm's top management appointment decision.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Every result is reported for both actual and usual hours; table 5 shows robustness to dropping multiple-employer observations, to weighting observations by distance from November, and to dropping interview weeks more than 6 months from November.

key_assumptions.assumption: Restricting the sample on the existence of a company peer group in the DLFS does not select managers on their appointment prospects, so the estimate on the restricted sample identifies the same quantity as on the full sample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered; the paper only notes that the number of observations falls because of missing observations for longest hours among peers.

implies_edges.from: the existence of a company peer group in the DLFS

threats_discussed: the hours observed in the DLFS interview week may come from, or be contaminated by, an employment relationship other than the one observed in the November register data
working hour observations more distant from November may be less relevant to the appointment decision
usual hours are more subject to measurement error (such as recall bias) than actual hours

table 5, cols. 5-6: observations weighted so that importance decreases linearly with the distance of the interview week to November
table 5, cols. 7-8: excluding observations more than 6 months from November (N = 28,809)
every specification reported for both actual and usual hours
every specification reported in a linear (h/100) and a nonlinear (hours-category dummy) form
table 9, cols. 1-4: table 4 reestimated on the restricted sample that has both h1 and h2, to show the restriction is inconsequential
a version of table 9 excluding individuals whose h2 crosses over to the following year (reported as qualitatively similar, not shown)

estimation.specification: equation (1), the baseline logit of a top management appointment on hours and controls, augmented with the longest-hours-among-peers dummy

source_table.value: Table 7, panel A. No Controls, col. (4), row 'longest hours among peers'

heterogeneity.dimension: hours concept (actual vs. usual) and inclusion of controls

register_source.value: IDA data merged with data from the DLFS

definition.value: The sample is split by sex and the Gicheva (2013, fig. 4) residualized hours-career profile is plotted separately for men and for women, with 90% confidence intervals, for both actual and usual hours.

timing.value: contemporaneous with the year-t hours observation

outcome.label: slope of the conditional hours-career profile (appointment residual plotted against hours)

register_source.value: DLFS hours merged with IDA appointment indicator

definition.value: The top management appointment dummy is regressed on all covariates except hours, and the residual is plotted against hours; the slope of that profile is the conditional relationship between hours and the odds of a top management appointment.

timing.value: appointment measured between t and t + 1, hours in t

units.value: slope of the appointment residual with respect to weekly hours; the figure's vertical axis runs from −.01 to .02 and the horizontal axis from 30 to 60 hours

magnitude.interpretation: The conditional hours-career profiles are upward sloping for both genders and their 90% confidence intervals suggest no statistically significant difference in slope.

estimand.target_population: Danish male and female managers who are not yet top managers; the quantity is the difference between the female and the male conditional hours-career slope
estimand.time_horizon: appointment between year t and year t + 1

population.description: Managers in the DLFS merged with IDA, estimated separately for men and for women
population.selection: The DLFS randomly samples Danish employees; the estimation sample conditions on holding a management position (but not a top management position) in year t.

identification.source_of_variation: difference between men and women in the covariate-adjusted relationship between hours and appointment odds; no exogenous variation in hours is used

key_assumptions.assumption: The residual from regressing the appointment dummy on every covariate except hours isolates the part of appointment odds that hours can explain, so that its profile against hours is the conditional hours-career relationship.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the two-step residualization procedure in fn. 25 and attributes the method to Gicheva (2013, fig. 4).

key_assumptions.assumption: Visual non-overlap, or overlap, of the 90% confidence bands of the two profiles is informative about whether the slopes differ.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper also runs the more standard test, adding gender-dummy-by-hours interaction terms to eq. (1), and reaches the same conclusion.

robustness_checks: the same conclusion is reached by adding gender-dummy-by-hours interaction terms to eq. (1)

estimator.value: two-step residualization (OLS/logit residual of appointment on all covariates except hours) plotted against hours, following Gicheva (2013, fig. 4), with 90% confidence intervals

estimation.specification: residualized version of eq. (1), estimated separately for men and for women, for both actual and usual hours

source_table.value: Figure 2, panels 'Men' and 'Women'

ambiguities: The figure prints confidence bands but no slope estimate or test statistic, so the null is recorded without a number.
theory_referenced: statistical discrimination / gender stereotyping as a demand-side explanation of the gender gap (Lundberg 2023)
outcomes_examined_not_reported: the gender-dummy-by-hours interaction estimates themselves - reported only in the online appendix

claims.statement: Adding interaction terms between a female dummy and hours to equation (1) yields no statistically significant effect on the odds of a top management appointment.

definition.value: The female and male samples are combined and eq. (1) is estimated augmented with interaction terms involving a gender dummy (female = 1 if the manager is female and 0 otherwise) and hours.

outcome.label: appoint (top management appointment between year t and year t + 1)

estimand.target_population: Danish managers who are not yet top managers; the quantity is the female-male difference in the return to hours
estimand.time_horizon: appointment between year t and year t + 1

population.description: The combined male and female manager sample from the DLFS merged with IDA
population.selection: The DLFS randomly samples Danish employees; the estimation sample conditions on holding a management position (but not a top management position) in year t.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates of eq. (1), any gender difference in the return to hours would show up in the interaction terms, so an insignificant interaction is evidence against a demand-side gender difference in the return to hours.

claims.statement: Female supervisory managers get almost no extra help in household production from their spouses, whereas male supervisory managers do: the gap between a supervisory manager's weekday work M-curve and the spouse's is large for men and near zero for women.

treatment.label: gender of the supervisory manager (female versus male)

register_source.value: Danish Time Use Surveys 2001 and 2008 (collected by the Danish Center for Social Science Research), questionnaire plus 10-minute time diaries

definition.value: Married supervisory managers in the Danish Time Use Surveys are split by sex. Supervisory managers in the Time Use Survey are described as roughly comparable to the top managers and managers of the register analysis.

timing.value: at the time of the 2001 or 2008 time use diary

outcome.label: gap between the supervisory manager's and the spouse's proportion working at a given 10-minute interval of the weekday

register_source.value: Danish Time Use Surveys 2001 and 2008: paired weekday 10-minute diaries of the manager and of the spouse

definition.value: For each 10-minute interval of the weekday the proportion of the group doing paid work is plotted; the outcome compared is the vertical distance between the supervisory manager's M-curve and the M-curve of his or her non-supervisor spouse. A large gap means the spouse is available for household production while the manager works.

timing.value: weekday diary day in 2001 or 2008

units.value: difference in the proportion of a group doing paid work in a 10-minute weekday interval (manager minus spouse)

magnitude.interpretation: Male supervisory managers display a perfectly symmetric M-curve lying well above their spouses' M-curve, while female supervisory managers and their spouses display nearly identical M-curves.

estimand.target_population: married Danish supervisory managers whose spouses are not supervisory managers
estimand.time_horizon: a single weekday diary day

population.description: 934 married supervisory managers in the 2001 and 2008 Danish Time Use Surveys whose spouses are not supervisory managers, together with those spouses; the surveys cover 10,624 households representative of the Danish population

female supervisory managers and their spouses
population.selection: Couples in which exactly one spouse is a supervisory manager; both spouses must have completed weekday and weekend diaries.

key_assumptions.assumption: Supervisory managers in the Danish Time Use Survey are comparable to the top managers and managers identified from the register data, so the time use evidence speaks to the sample of the regression analysis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper asserts the comparability but offers no crosswalk between the Time Use Survey occupation code and the register hierarchy code.

key_assumptions.assumption: Time spent not doing paid work during the weekday is a usable proxy for availability for household production, so a spouse whose M-curve lies below the manager's is supplying extra household production.
Couples are not selected into the manager-gender comparison on their household division of labor; no covariates are adjusted for.

implies_edges.from: being a married couple with exactly one supervisory manager

robustness_checks: figure 4 repeats the comparison for the 133 power couples in which both spouses are supervisory managers

estimator.value: unconditional group means of a 0/1 'doing paid work' indicator by 10-minute weekday interval; no regression

estimation.specification: proportion of each group working, plotted by time of weekday in 10-minute intervals, for supervisory managers and for their non-supervisor spouses, separately by the manager's sex

mediators_claimed: gendered division of labor in household production

nodes: household production supplied by the spouse
